text:
No direct controlled comparison was found between recent-window mean pooling, exponential recency pooling, and learned long/short-term gates with cosine-agreement weighting in SASRec. [SASRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.09781) reports attention favoring recent actions on sparse datasets and longer dependencies on dense datasets. [SLi-Rec](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/uploads/prod/2019/07/IJCAI19-ready_v1.pdf) provides adjacent evidence: adaptive fusion outperformed fixed mixtures; short-term modeling beat long-term modeling, and naive combinations sometimes hurt. These results support testing adaptive fusion, but do not establish superiority for the proposed agreement mechanism or robustness to abrupt shifts.

Popularity remains a confound. Dot products can favor popular items through embedding norms; cosine removes that norm contribution ([Google documentation](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/recommendation/overview/candidate-generation)). However, popularity also affects embedding directions through unequal interaction gradients ([Ren et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.01154)). Thus, interaction-trained cosine agreement indicates collaborative compatibility, not independently verified semantic repeated interest. Mechanistic concern: agreement with a long-history centroid could suppress a novel recent interest. For weights softmax(cosine/τ), smaller τ concentrates support; larger τ approaches uniform pooling over eligible positions. [Sampled-softmax experiments](https://wujcan.github.io/papers/tois-ssm.pdf) show temperature sensitivity, although their loss-temperature findings do not directly validate pooling temperature. A positive global temperature applied only to final ranking scores leaves ordering unchanged.

Recommended controls: unchanged SASRec; last-item support; equal-weight recent windows; exponential decay; fixed long/short mixtures; learned gates without agreement; agreement without gates; popularity-only and popularity-adjusted scores. Match training and validation budgets. Diagnose head/tail performance, recommendation popularity, and recent-versus-old disagreement using public histories; independently check title/description similarity before claiming semantics. Treat disagreement as a shift proxy, not observed intent.
